clue.text: Where members sit with girls who work in hotels?

definitions.note: a phrase standing for the people who do this job

parts.note: a legislative chamber is the room where members of parliament sit
maids is an old word for girls or young women

explanation.surface: A question about where politicians sit alongside young women employed in hotels.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the closing phrase, read as 'people who work in hotels'; the question mark flags the whimsical build.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotel staff who clean and make up the bedrooms are called by this name.

clue.text: Seize the remedy, drinking a pint

indicators.note: something drinking another takes it inside, so the remedy word swallows the other letters

parts.note: a cure is a remedy for an illness

explanation.surface: Grab the medicine that has a pint of beer in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinking' puts A and PT inside CURE.
explanation.definitionFit: To seize something is to take hold of it by force, as when soldiers take a town.

parts.note: a Highlander comes from the north of Scotland, so is a Scot

explanation.surface: Asking which royal racecourse might suit someone from the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.walkthrough: Royal Ascot is the famous racecourse and meeting in Berkshire, England, attended by the royal family.
explanation.definitionFit: The racecourse near Windsor holds the Royal meeting each June, a fixture of the British social season.

clue.text: Start batting the way team attack

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, here the opening of the word batting

parts.note: a road is a way to travel along
a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A cricket team begins batting in an aggressive manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start' takes B from 'batting'; batting is cricket, but here only its first letter counts.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is a fierce verbal onslaught, originally a volley from all the guns on one side of a warship.

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so the sheep word takes in the letter for love

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep
love means zero in tennis scoring, shown as the letter O

explanation.surface: A flock of sheep tolerates affection, yet strays off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accept' puts O inside RAM.
explanation.definitionFit: To roam is to travel about aimlessly, a synonym for straying around.

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
to spice something up is to add excitement, so spices

explanation.surface: An exclamation that gold makes things more thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: Auspices are omens; the word comes from Roman augurs reading signs from the flight of birds.
explanation.definitionFit: In Roman times omens from birds were read as portents, and the word kept that sense of favourable omens.

clue.text: Cacophony covering soldiers that run out

indicators.note: one thing covering another wraps around it, so the noise word goes round the soldiers

parts.note: a din is a loud discordant noise
RA, the Royal Artillery, is a crossword stand-in for soldiers

explanation.surface: A racket drowns out troops who are running away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'covering' puts RA inside DIN; 'that' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To drain is to let liquid flow away until empty, so to empty or exhaust.

parts.note: MO, medical officer, is a crossword stand-in for a doctor

indicators.note: playing here means acting up or performing freely, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive s is dropped, leaving the letters of on and Eton

explanation.surface: A physician walks onto the sports field of Eton College.
explanation.walkthrough: Eton is a famous English private school; its 'playing pitch' in the surface becomes a single unvarying musical pitch, and 'playing' rearranges ON ETON to NOTONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A voice or note that stays at one level throughout has a single unvarying tone.

explanation.surface: Asking about the state of affairs in the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: States means conditions, as in states of mind; and the States is an informal name for the USA.

indicators.note: to develop is to grow or change form, so these letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Watchful police officers build up their bodies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'develop' rearranges ALERT COPS.
explanation.definitionFit: The pectorals are the chest muscles, known in gyms as pecs.

clue.text: Assume there'll be a day to make a choice

parts.note: to opt is to choose

explanation.surface: Suppose a day will come when a decision must be made.
explanation.definitionFit: To adopt a role or manner is to take it on, so to assume it.

clue.text: A French trim is a bit messy

parts.note: un is the French word for a
trim as an adjective means neat or tidy

explanation.surface: A French haircut looks slightly scruffy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trim' looks like a haircut but is the adjective meaning neat.
explanation.definitionFit: Untidy describes things not in order, a mild word for disorderly.

clue.text: It shows the way to trace the mail

parts.note: a trace is a sign or slight indication of something
post is the British word for mail

explanation.surface: A way to track down letters sent through the postal service.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside pointer with arms names places and gives directions to travellers.

clue.text: Poor clue one initially developed for an old mathematician

indicators.note: poor here means badly made, so the letters of clue are reworked

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: initially picks out the opening letter of the following word, developed

explanation.surface: A badly written crossword clue was devised for an ancient maths scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' rearranges CLUE to EUCL; then I and the D from 'developed' follow.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek geometer of Alexandria wrote the Elements around 300 BC.

indicators.note: welcoming means taking someone in, so the embrace word takes in the Spanish article

parts.note: a caress is a gentle embrace
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A clumsy hug greets the people of Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'welcoming' puts EL inside CARESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Careless work is slapdash, done without due attention.

clue.text: Rescue workers looking embarrassed and angry

parts.note: someone embarrassed goes red in the face
cross is an informal word for angry

explanation.surface: Emergency helpers look both flushed and irritated.
explanation.definitionFit: The international humanitarian organisation sends aid workers to disasters and war zones.

clue.text: A pedantic sort was in charge

indicators.note: to sort is to arrange, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A nit-picking type of person used to lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort' looks like a noun (a type of person) but is the anagram signal on A PEDANTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: To have captained a team or ship is to have led it as skipper.

indicators.note: after places the angry word behind the counter word

parts.note: a bar is a counter where drinks are served
to rage is to get angry, so rages

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper following a counter-attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'counter attacks' reads as one military phrase, but 'counter' is BAR and 'attacks' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Barrages are heavy bombardments of artillery fire, or figuratively a torrent of questions.

indicators.note: back means the knock word is read in the reverse direction

parts.note: a rap is a sharp knock

indicators.note: processed means treated or changed, so the letters of means are rearranged

explanation.surface: Gulping down some factory-made cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns RAP into PAR; 'processed' rearranges MEANS to MESAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A hard Italian variety from Parma, often grated over pasta.

indicators.note: reportedly signals that the word is heard rather than read

parts.note: a pact is an agreement

explanation.surface: Being completely in accord, so people say.
explanation.definitionFit: A crammed room or suitcase has no space left in it.

explanation.surface: Asking whether butter is made on a farm in the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: A spread is US usage for a large ranch; and butter is something smeared on bread.

clue.text: Swell, seeing daughter first to finish

parts.note: first is written 1st, with the digit 1 read as the letter I
an end is a finish

explanation.surface: Puffing up as the daughter is seen first to the finishing line.
explanation.walkthrough: 1ST, with the 1 taken as I, is a common crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: To distend is to stretch out and bulge from pressure inside, as a bloated stomach does.

parts.note: a collie is a breed of sheepdog
RY, short for railway, stands for tracks

explanation.surface: A dog leaves its paw prints inside a hole in the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link; 'tracks' looks like a verb but is the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: A coal mine is called a pit in Britain, with its works and buildings.

parts.note: reads as a building project stopped in the North, but describes a house made of blocks of snow in the Arctic

explanation.definitionFit: Inuit shelters built from cut blocks of compacted snow are found in the Arctic.

clue.text: Sticks, being tense in front of opponents at table

indicators.note: in front of places the tense word before the opponents

parts.note: the past is a grammatical tense
in bridge, East and South sit opposite partners and play against each other, abbreviated E and S

explanation.surface: Uses glue, nervous in front of rivals at the card table.
explanation.walkthrough: In the card game bridge, players are named North, South, East and West; E and S are on opposing sides.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastes are adhesives, and to paste is to glue something in place.

parts.note: ST, for saint, is the crossword stand-in for a good man

explanation.surface: Raise a glass to a decent fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: ST, for saint, is the crossword convention for a good man; the question mark flags the surface's toast to a decent fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise a glass in someone's honour is a celebratory salute.

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a live wire is electrically charged

explanation.surface: An exclamation that something powered up is evil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses LIVE in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe morally bad, sinful conduct.

parts.note: ease is comfort and freedom from strain

explanation.surface: A broad-minded backer gives reassurance.
explanation.definitionFit: An artist's stand holds the canvas up while painting.

parts.note: the past tense of baptising with a name, read as the description of a first name given at birth

explanation.definitionFit: The first name bestowed at baptism, as opposed to a surname, is what a christening gives.

clue.text: Made firm adapt to island code

indicators.note: to adapt is to alter, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fixing things by modifying the island's postal code.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapt' rearranges TO ISLAND CODE.
explanation.definitionFit: To consolidate is to strengthen or combine into a solid whole.
